questions.q: According to this lesson, what changes when a governance analyst explains the same underlying fact to an executive versus a technical team?
options: The facts themselves should be different for each audience
Nothing should change; every audience should get an identical technical deep-dive
Which part of the message leads and how much detail is given first — not the underlying facts themselves
Only executives should ever be told the truth about project status
questions.explain: Audience layering adjusts which part of a message leads and how much detail comes first, based on who's listening — the underlying facts stay the same.

questions.q: What does an executive sponsor need first, according to this lesson's audience table?
options: The business impact and the decision needed from them, in one or two sentences
A step-by-step walkthrough of the tool used to implement the control
A history of every meeting held about the project so far
A list of every field name involved in the project
questions.explain: Executives need the business impact and the decision they're being asked to make first — implementation detail can follow if they ask for it, but it shouldn't lead.

questions.q: What are the four parts of the short governance update structure this lesson recommends?
options: A joke, a long history lesson, a technical diagram, and a thank-you
The ask first, followed by three paragraphs of background before the headline
The headline, the "so what" for that listener, the ask (if any), and the next checkpoint
Only a headline — nothing else should be included in a short update
questions.explain: The lesson's four-part structure is: headline (current state), the "so what" (why it matters to this listener), the ask if there is one, and the next checkpoint.

questions.q: What does the sample executive update in this lesson deliberately leave out?
options: When the sponsor will hear an update next
The business consequence of the work completed so far
How the classification scheme was built and the name of the tool used to tag columns
The current status of the project
questions.explain: The sample update states current status, business consequence, and next checkpoint, but deliberately omits implementation detail like the tool name or how the scheme was built — detail an executive didn't ask for.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend stating an ask explicitly rather than writing something vague like "thoughts welcome"?
options: Because "thoughts welcome" is considered rude in a business context
Because every governance update must avoid asking for anything at all
Because a vague phrase doesn't make clear whether a specific decision or approval is actually needed, by when
Because stakeholders are never willing to give approvals in writing
questions.explain: An explicit ask ("I need your approval by Friday") tells the reader exactly what action is needed and by when, which a vague phrase like "thoughts welcome" does not.
